newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia banks on hybrid corn to reduce imports.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia banks on hybrid corn to reduce imports.

text.p: Indonesia expects a substantial increase in corn output this year with the introduction of a hybrid strain and hopes the high-yielding variety will help it reduce imports, government officials and traders said on Friday.
Syamsuddin Abbas, head of the farmers' guidance division in the agriculture ministry, said production was forecast to total 9.2 million tonnes this year against 8.0 million in 1996.
"Indonesia imported about 1.6 million tonnes of corn in 1996, and we are hoping to reduce the volume this year following the introduction of the hybrid variety," he told Reuters.
Corn is used for animal feed and is also consumed by humans as food and in the form of oil.
Indonesia's President Suharto, who takes a personal interest in agricultural commodities, said late last year the country should take steps to reduce corn imports.
"Our intention is to become self-sufficient in corn. But it will depend on the crop. There might be times when we import and times when we export when we have extra," Syamsuddin said.
He said 351,000 hectares had been planted with the hybrid strain, and a further 144,000 hectares would be planted with the strain over the next two months.
"We will plant another 390,000 hectares with hybrid corn between April and September," he said. "A total of 900,000 hectares will be planted with hybrid corn in 1998."
He said the hybrid strain produces an average five tonnes per hectare compared with 2.2 to 2.5 tonnes offered by the ordinary variety.
Syamsuddin said the 351,000 hectares already planted with the high-yielding variety would be ready for harvest in the first quarter of this year.
Traders said Indonesia's desire to become self-sufficient in corn was understandable in view of the high imports, but they added it was an ambitious target.

"Indonesia has one of the lowest per capita consumptions of chicken in Southeast Asia at 3.5 kg, compared with twice that in the Philippines whose per capita income is only slightly higher than Indonesia's," one senior foreign corn trader said.
"As Indonesia becomes more affluent, its citizens' preference for chicken will grow. This means the demand for corn is going to grow," he said.
Another trader said he expected domestic corn production growth to be matched by an increase in demand, adding that Indonesia was likely to continue importing corn.
"I don't see a situation where Indonesia can reduce corn imports very substantially," he said.

"The domestic price of corn must be profitable enough for farmers to grow it, and all indications in the international markets are that prices will be heading south because of good crops in many corn exporting countries," he said.
